items.title: Medieval Europeans knew the Earth was round
items.claim: The idea that 'medieval people thought the Earth was flat' was popularised in the 19th century. Who is most responsible for spreading it?

options.text: Galileo, in his trial defence of 1633
Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Columbus, which fabricated a debate at Salamanca about whether Columbus would sail off the edge
Karl Marx, as part of his critique of religion

items.reveal:
Bede (8th century), Aquinas (13th century), Dante (14th century) and the entire scholastic tradition assumed a spherical Earth — it was Aristotelian orthodoxy reinforced by Ptolemy. Columbus's argument with the Salamanca scholars was about the Earth's circumference, not its shape; they thought (correctly) it was too large to sail to Asia westward.

Washington Irving's 'A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus' (1828) was a partly fictionalised popular biography. It invented the flat-Earth debate to make Columbus look more visionary. The myth then became a stock anti-medieval, anti-Catholic talking point in the late 19th century (notably John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White).
items.why: Historiography matters. The 'Dark Ages' frame and the flat-Earth myth are products of later polemic, not medieval thought. The conflict-between-science-and-religion narrative is largely a 19th-century construction.

items.title: Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 CE but converted slowly
items.claim: When did the Roman Empire become Christian?

options.text: Constantine made Christianity the state religion in 312

The Edict of Milan (313) granted religious toleration; Constantine increasingly favoured Christianity but was baptised only on his deathbed in 337; Theodosius I made Christianity the state religion by the Edict of Thessalonica in 380
The empire remained pagan until 600 CE

items.reveal:
Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (28 October 312) over Maxentius came after a reported vision of the Chi-Rho symbol with 'in hoc signo vinces' (in this sign you will conquer). The Edict of Milan, agreed with Licinius in 313, granted religious toleration to all.

Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea (325) and built churches across the empire. He moved the capital to Constantinople (founded 330). He was baptised on his deathbed in 337 by an Arian bishop, Eusebius of Nicomedia.

The Edict of Thessalonica (380) under Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion. Pagan worship was progressively restricted; the Olympic Games were banned in 393.
items.why: Religious change at imperial scale is a process, not a moment. The 67 years between Milan and Thessalonica saw a tolerant empire become a Christian one — a transformation studied by every subsequent religious-political shift.

items.title: Thomas More's 'Utopia' (1516) coined the word
items.claim: What did Thomas More publish in 1516?

options.text: A history of the Wars of the Roses

'Utopia' — a Latin work describing a fictional island society, coining the word from Greek 'ou-topos' (no place) and 'eu-topos' (good place); a humanist critique of European politics, property and religion
A defence of the medieval feudal system

items.reveal_title: No place that critiques every place
items.reveal:
'Utopia' was written in Latin and first printed at Louvain in 1516. The Utopians hold property in common, work six hours a day, practise religious toleration and choose elected officials. The book mixes serious proposal with deliberate ambiguity — More may or may not endorse his fictional society.

More was Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII from 1529 to 1532, resigning over the king's annulment plans. He refused the Oath of Succession (1534) and was executed on 6 July 1535 with the famous 'King's good servant, but God's first.'

He was canonised in 1935. The word 'utopia' entered every European language as a term for an imagined ideal society.
items.why: Renaissance humanism produced political ideas centuries ahead of their reception. 'Utopia' has been read by socialists, anarchists, Catholics and modern progressives — each finding their own programme in More's deliberately ambiguous text.
